title: Flight booking schema in PostgreSQL
idea: The flight schema maps the Java model to tables so PostgreSQL enforces the rules: fare counts never drop below zero, and each seat gets one ticket per flight.

analogy.text: A box office tally board with one chalk number per price tier. Only one clerk may hold the chalk, and the number cannot drop below zero.
analogy.breaks: The row lock lasts milliseconds; a HELD booking lasts fifteen minutes.

points: `fare_class.seats_left` has a CHECK, so overselling fails even if code forgets.
A UNIQUE on `(flight_id, seat_no)` gives each seat one ticket; NULL seats stay allowed.
One conditional UPDATE locks the fare row, checks the count, and subtracts.
Index `flight_search` serves search; a partial index on HELD serves the sweeper.

steps.caption: Y-SAVER has one seat left. Two transactions want it at the same moment.
PNR-7's UPDATE finds the row, locks it, sees 1 is enough, and writes 0.
PNR-9's UPDATE reaches the same row and must wait for the lock.
PNR-7 inserts its HELD booking and commits. The lock is released.
PNR-9 wakes and re-checks the condition on the new row: 0 is not enough.
Zero rows updated means refuse. PNR-9 rolls back and holds nothing.
Fifteen minutes later PNR-7 has not paid. The sweeper expires it and adds the seat back.

code.title: Tables and constraints
code.caption: The schema on a real PostgreSQL 18, then five bad writes that the database refuses by itself.

walk.text: Fixed layout: aircraft and its seats. Enums are TEXT with a CHECK.
A flight refuses loop routes; `flight_search` serves the search by route and time.
`fare_class` keeps money as BIGINT and bounds `seats_left` between 0 and total.
`booking` checks passenger count and status; the partial index serves the sweeper.
One ticket per passenger per PNR, and one ticket per seat per flight.
Each bad write prints the Postgres error code and the constraint that stopped it.
A second ticket with no seat is fine: UNIQUE treats NULLs as distinct.

code.title: Hold and sweep
code.caption: Two parallel holds race for the last seat; then the sweeper returns expired seats. The tables are trimmed so the race stays short.

walk.text: The conditional UPDATE locks the fare row and subtracts only if enough seats remain.
Zero rows updated means not enough seats: roll back and refuse.
Otherwise insert the HELD booking with a 15-minute deadline and commit; any error rolls back.
One statement expires old holds and adds their seats back per fare.
Two clients race for one seat; print how many won, never who.
Three of four J-FLEX seats are held; two more are refused; sweeps return seats.

pitfalls: Do not `SELECT` the count and `UPDATE` later; put the check inside the UPDATE.
Keep the CHECK on `seats_left` anyway; it catches bugs your code missed.
Every index should name the query it serves; drop the ones that serve none.

quiz.q: What does reserve.mjs print for 2 pax on J-FLEX?
quiz.why: J-FLEX had 4 seats and PNR-10 took 3. The UPDATE condition `seats_left >= 2` fails on 1, so no row updates and `holdFare` returns false.

takeaway: Put the seat check inside the UPDATE; let constraints catch the rest.

starters: Why does PNR-9 see 0 after waiting instead of the old 1?
Should seat assignment lock rows like the fare count does?
How would I add overbooking to this schema later?
